newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Swiss find Holocaust heirs to 10 million francs.
newsitem.headline: Swiss find Holocaust heirs to 10 million francs.

text.p: Swiss banks have found the heirs to 10 million Swiss francs ($6.8 million) left by Holocaust victims - about a quarter of dormant World War Two-era accounts identified last year, the banking ombudsman said on Tuesday.

Hanspeter Haeni's ombudsman agency also rejected criticism by World Jewish Congress (WJC) officials and U.S. Senator Alfonse D'Amato that it had moved too slowly in matching lost accounts to claims pouring in from family members.
"This has been a pioneer effort with no model in the entire world for a similar undertaking," said Leon Schlumpf, head of the Swiss Banking Ombudsman Foundation that runs Haeni's office.
Switzerland's Jewish Federation welcomed the interim finding as a basis for continuing the sweep that started in early 1996.
"This is positive news that shows it was justified to demand a search," Thomas Lyssy, vice-president of the SIG federation, told Reuters.

Based on often sketchy information submitted by relatives, Haeni said his office had so far found 17 million Swiss francs in 28 accounts deemed dormant, meaning the banks had not heard from the owners for at least 10 years.
Of those, nine cases involved Jewish account owners who had not been heard from since World War Two ended in 1945, making it likely they were victims of the Holocaust.

"In these nine cases, assets with a total value of around 10 million Swiss francs are involved, a significant percentage of which was accounted for by a single testator," Haeni told a news conference on results as of the end of May.
Swiss banks last year put the total of all pre-1945 dormant accounts -- not just those opened by Jews -- at around 40 million Swiss francs.
Haeni said he assumed the 10 million he has found were part of the 40 million identified by the banks but added that some dormant accounts may never be claimed.
"To put it brutally, the Nazis did a thorough job and there may be no heirs at all for some assets," he said.
Jewish groups have alleged Swiss banks had hoarded billions of dollars in deposits by Holocaust victims, a figure the banks have dismissed as wildly inflated.
Haeni declined to give the news conference any more information about the one big account that makes up a large part of the 10 million figure, saying he was bound to protect each owner's privacy.

The findings were a big step forward since last November, when Haeni said the hunt for unclaimed wealth in Swiss bank vaults had uncovered valid claims for only 1.6 million francs, of which only 11,000 francs was held by Jews.
The low figure prompted WJC officials and D'Amato, whose Senate Banking Committee is probing Switzerland, to question whether Haeni's office was able to carry out the search.

Under pressure to speed up the search for accounts left by victims of the Nazis, Swiss banks agreed two weeks ago to hand over Haeni's job to an independent panel to be set up soon by the banks, Swiss regulators and a joint Swiss-Jewish commission headed by former U.S. central bank chief Paul Volcker.

The banks also said they would publish a list of names of pre-1945 dormant accounts on July 23, using the Internet and other media to spread the information internationally so Holocaust survivors or their heirs could come forward. ($ = 1.460 Swiss Francs)
